q: Straight fine scissors with pointed tips; may be curved.
u: Dissects bulbar conjunctiva, e.g. conjunctival flap in cataract, trabeculectomy, squint, retinal detachment and enucleation operations; may cut suture ends and other tissues such as Tenon's capsule, pterygium and skin edges.
note: Conjunctival Scissors — Identification: It is a straight fine scissors with pointed tips. It may be curved. Uses: a) It is used to dissect the bulbar conjunctiva in some operations. Conjunctival flap in cataract operation: Here the flap may be limbal-based or fornix-based. Limbal-based flap: The conjunctiva is cut few mm away from the limbus and then it is reflected over the cornea from its attached base at the limbus. Fornix-based flap: The conjunctiva is cut at the limbus and retracted towards the fornix. Fornix-based flap is better than limbal-based flap. Conjunctival flap in trabeculectomy operation, squint, retinal detachment, enucleation operation, etc. b) It may be used to cut the suture ends. c) It is used to cut other tissues, e.g. Tenon's capsule, pterygium, skin edges, etc.

q: Image not verified — text only. Small curved spring scissors with sharp small blades.
u: Extends ab-externo section in cataract operation; cuts corneal button in keratoplasty; may cut 8-0 suture ends and iris for iridectomy.
note: Corneal Spring Scissors (Universal) — Identification: It is a small curved spring scissors with sharp small blades. It is called universal, as it is used to cut both right and left half of the section (right half means temporal half of right cornea and nasal half of left cornea, and vice versa). Uses: a) To extend ab-externo section in cataract operation. b) To cut the corneal button from the donor and recipient eyes in case of keratoplasty. c) It may be used to cut the 8-0 suture ends. d) It may be used to cut the iris for iridectomy.

q: Butterfly-shaped spring scissors; blades bent at 60 degrees to the handle; two wings for index finger and thumb; one blade pointed, one rounded.
u: Cuts iris tissue in iridectomy; anterior/open-sky vitrectomy if vitreous loss; cuts trabecular tissue with part of sclera in trabeculectomy; may cut 8.0 or 10-0 suture ends; during corneoscleral suturing.
note: De Wecker's Iris Scissors — Identification: It is a butterfly-shaped spring scissors with the cutting blades bent at an angle of 60 degrees with the handle. On the handle, there are two wings for index finger and thumb. Its one blade has pointed tip and the other blade has rounded tip. Method: Scissors are held in such a way that the plane of blade lies at the same plane as of iris, with the handle almost vertical. Uses: a) It is used to cut a piece of iris tissue in iridectomy. b) It is used for anterior or open-sky vitrectomy, if there is any vitreous loss during cataract extraction. c) It is used to cut the trabecular tissue with a part of sclera in trabeculectomy operation. d) It may be used to cut the suture ends (8.0 or 10-0 sutures). e) During corneoscleral suturing.

q: Central circular optic with two side haptics; rigid PMMA or foldable (silicone, acrylic, hydrogel, collamer) or rollable (hydrogel).
u: Replaces the crystalline lens in cataract surgery; power calculated by the SRK formula (see added note).
note: Intraocular Lens — Diameter: Optic 5-7 mm; Haptic 12 mm. Types: Anterior chamber IOL, Posterior chamber IOL, Iris-supported. Based on material: Rigid IOL (PMMA). Foldable IOL (silicon, acrylic, hydrogel, collamer). Rollable IOL (hydrogel). Power of IOL (SRK formula): P=A-2.5L-0.9K Where: P - power of IOL. A - a constant which is specific for each lens type. L - axial length of eyeball in mm. K - average corneal curvature. Video note — Rigid Intraocular Lens (Non-Foldable IOL): Material: PMMA (Polymethylmethacrylate). Parts: A central circular optic and two side haptics (may have positioning/dialing holes). Used in SICS and ECCE.

q: Cross-cylinder lens with a handle; commonly ±0.25 D and ±0.50 D.
u: Verifies strength and axis of a cylindrical lens.
note: Jackson's Cross Cylinder — Heading visible; description continues on the next page. (continued below) Jackson's Cross Cylinder — Used to verify strength and axis of cylindrical lens. Commonly used cross cylinders are of ±0.25 D and ±0.50 D.

q: Image not verified — text only. Many red glass rods set together in a metallic disc.
u: Macular function test, diplopia.
note: Maddox Rod — Consists of many glass rods of red colour set together in a metallic disc. Uses: Macular function test, diplopia.

q: Image not verified — text only. Red lens in front of right eye and green lens in front of left eye; patient views a box with 4 lights — 1 red, 2 green, white.
u: Diplopia charting; Worth's four-dot test.
note: Red Green Goggles — For diplopia charting. Worth's four-dot test: Patient wears red lens in front of right eye and green lens in front of left eye and views a box with 4 lights - 1 red, 2 green, white (interpretation - refer Khurana).

q: Thin straight blade with sharp pointed tip and a cutting edge; other edge blunt; may have sliding case to protect the tip.
u: Ab-interno section in cataract operation; optical iridectomy; paracentesis; glaucoma iridectomy; suture removal; pterygium/chalazion dissection; 4-point iridotomy in iris bombe.
note: Von Graefe's Cataract Knife — Identification: It has a thin straight blade with sharp pointed tip and a cutting edge, the other edge is blunt. The blade may be thin or thick. It may have sliding case arrangement where the sharp blade end is kept in a cover to protect its tip when it is not in use. Uses: a) Ab-interno section in case of cataract operation. b) Optical iridectomy. c) Paracentesis. d) Glaucoma iridectomy. e) Suture removal after cataract operation. f) In pterygium operation to dissect the head, or in chalazion operation to give incision. g) 4-point iridotomy in iris bombe (quadri-puncture).

q: Medium-size instrument with two jaw-like plates at the tip to catch a razor blade firmly; catch at the other end for better grip.
u: Breaks a carbon-steel razor blade into fragments for use like a Bard-Parker knife blade; at least 8 fragments from one blade.
note: Blade Breaker — Identification: It is an instrument to break the razor blade (must be a carbon steel blade - e.g. 'Bharat' blade). It is of medium size, with two jaw-like plates at its tip to catch the razor blade firmly. The other end of the instrument has a catch for better grip of the blade. At least 8 blade-fragments can be made from a single razor blade. Advantages: a) It is cheaper than any other knife-blade. b) It is sharper than No. 11 or No. 15. Disadvantages: As only the breakable carbon-steel razor blade is used - rust formation is a problem. Uses: Blade breaker with razor blade-fragments has the same uses as Bard Parker handle with knife. Instruments used for corneoscleral section are: a) Cataract Knife. b) Bard Parker knife. c) Blade breaker with razor blade. d) Disposable super-blades. e) Keratome. f) Diamond knife.

q: Image not verified — text only. Curved or angular forceps with fine limbs, having 1:2 teeth at its tip; thicker and stout; named after the hummingbird.
u: Holds corneal/scleral lip during suturing and holds iris for peripheral iridectomy.
note: Colibri Forceps — Identification: It is a curved or angular forceps with fine limbs, having 1:2 teeth at its tip. It is thicker and stout. Uses (Colibri and St. Martin's have similar uses): a) To hold the cornea and scleral lips during corneoscleral suturing after cataract surgery, and corneal lips in repair of penetrating injury or wound closure in keratoplasty. b) It is also used to hold the scleral lip for dissection and scleral suturing (as in trabeculectomy operation). c) It is used to hold the corneal lip in cataract operation to extend the section with a knife. d) To lift the cornea upwards during application of the cryoprobe. e) It may be used in iridectomy. Video note — Colibri Forceps & Peripheral Iridectomy (PI): Colibri Forceps: Design: Named after the hummingbird (Colibri); has a characteristic angled shape with very fine 1x2 teeth at the tip (and a tying platform). Uses: Holding the corneal or scleral lip while passing sutures in cataract surgery, corneal laceration repair, or penetrating keratoplasty. Holding the iris to perform a Peripheral Iridectomy (PI). Clinical Discussion: Peripheral Iridectomy (PI) vs. Laser Iridotomy: Laser Iridotomy: Performed non-invasively using an Nd:YAG Laser (1064 nm, photodisruption/cutting laser). Surgical Iridectomy: Mechanical excision of a piece of peripheral iris using Colibri/Iris forceps and Vannas/De Wecker's scissors. Indications for Peripheral Iridectomy (PI): 1. Primary Angle-Closure Glaucoma (PACG): Relieves pupillary block (which maximally occurs in a mid-dilated pupil of 4-5 mm, trapping aqueous humor in the posterior chamber and causing iris bombe). PI creates an alternative bypass channel for aqueous to flow from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber. 2. Prophylactic PI in the fellow eye of a patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma. 3. As part of Trabeculectomy (Glaucoma Filtration Surgery): Done at the sclerostomy site (usually superiorly at 12 o'clock) so the iris does not plug or block the internal trabeculectomy ostium. 4. Complicated Cataract Surgery: E.g., when implanting an ACIOL (Anterior Chamber IOL) or Iris-claw lens to prevent pupillary block, or in cases of iris prolapse / shallow AC. 5. Excision of small iris tumors or removal of intracameral foreign bodies.

q: Straight, small but stout forceps with 1:2 teeth at its fine tip.
u: Holds cornea/scleral lips during suturing, scleral lip for dissection/suturing, corneal lip to extend section, lifts cornea for cryoprobe, may be used in iridectomy.
note: St. Martin's Forceps — Identification: It is a straight, small but stout forceps with 1:2 teeth at its fine tip. Uses (both Colibri and St. Martin's have similar uses): a) To hold the cornea and scleral lips during corneoscleral suturing after cataract surgery, and corneal lips in repair of penetrating injury or wound closure in keratoplasty. b) It is also used to hold the scleral lip for dissection and scleral suturing (as in trabeculectomy operation). c) It is used to hold the corneal lip in cataract operation to extend the section with a knife. d) To lift the cornea upwards during application of the cryoprobe. e) It may be used in iridectomy. This is a separate card from the Fixation forceps card, to avoid mixing the St. Martin's fixation note with this instrument. Video 2 fixation variant note (in addition to the pages note above): Lim's / St. Martin's / Pierce Hoskins Corneoscleral & Conjunctival Fixation Forceps: Design: Fine 1x2 toothed forceps at the tip. Uses: Holding and fixing the conjunctiva, Tenon's capsule, or scleral edge during peritomy, suturing, or globe fixation. This Video 2 fixation variant is in addition to, not a replacement for, the St. Martin's pages note above.

q: Two limbs with three curved pins on each for engaging skin incision edges; limbs kept retracted with a fixing screw.
u: Retracts skin during surgery on the lacrimal sac (e.g. DCT or DCR).
note: Self-Retaining Lacrimal Wound (Muller's) Retractor — Identification: Made up of two limbs with three curved pins on each for engaging the edges of the skin incision. The limbs are kept in a retracted position with the help of a fixing screw. Uses: To retract the skin during surgery on the lacrimal sac (e.g. DCT or DCR). Video note — Muller's Self-Retaining Hemostatic Lacrimal Sac Retractor: Design: Self-retaining retractor with 3x3 curved prongs and a screw lock. Uses: Retracts skin and orbicularis oculi muscle edges and achieves hemostasis (by compressing angular/cutaneous vessels) during DCT (Dacryocystectomy) and DCR (Dacryocystorhinostomy) for chronic dacryocystitis.

q: Image not verified — text only. Small lancet-shaped needle with sharp cutting edges resembling a small keratome; has a guard to prevent inadvertent injury to deeper structures.
u: For paracentesis; to make very small corneoscleral incisions.
note: Paracentesis Needle — Identification: It is a small lancet-shaped needle with sharp cutting edges resembling in appearance to a small keratome. It has got a guard to prevent inadvertent injury to the deeper structures. Uses: a) For paracentesis. b) To make very small corneoscleral incisions.

q: Spring-action forceps with short, blunt and curved blades having smooth edges and tips with platform (no teeth or serrations).
u: Holds optic of non-foldable PMMA IOL during implantation.
note: IOL Holding Forceps — Identification: It is a spring action forceps with short, blunt and curved blades having smooth edges and tips with platform (no teeth or serrations). Uses: To hold optic of non-foldable PMMA IOL during implantation.

q: Image not verified — text only. Cartridge and injector used to fold and inject a foldable IOL through a small incision.
u: Folds and injects a foldable IOL through a small incision (< 3 mm) directly into the capsular bag in phacoemulsification.
note: Foldable IOL Cartridge and Injector — Use: Used in Phacoemulsification to fold and inject a foldable IOL through a small incision (< 3 mm) directly into the capsular bag. Foldable IOL Materials: Acrylic (Hydrophobic or Hydrophilic), Silicone, Hydrogel.

q: Indentation tonometer: curved footplate, central plunger, holding bracket/handle, inclined scale with pointer, detachable weights (5.5 g fixed, plus 7.5 g, 10 g, 15 g).
u: Measures IOP by indentation; scale reading converted via Friedenwald's Conversion Chart/Table.
note: Schiotz Indentation Tonometer — Principle: Indentation Tonometry - measures how much a weighted plunger indents the anesthetized cornea; a softer eye (low IOP) indents more, giving a higher scale reading, and vice versa. Components: Curved footplate, central plunger, holding bracket/handle, inclined scale with pointer, and detachable weights (5.5 g fixed on plunger, plus 7.5 g, 10 g, and 15 g additional weights). Procedure Note: The scale reading is converted into Intraocular Pressure (mmHg) using Friedenwald's Conversion Chart/Table.

q: Image not verified — text only. Black opaque disc with a small central aperture (1-1.5 mm).
u: Differentiates refractive errors from organic media opacities or retinal/macular diseases.
note: Pinhole (PH) — Design: Black opaque disc with a small central aperture (1-1.5 mm). Principle: Allows only the central paraxial rays of light to pass straight through the nodal point/optical center of the eye without requiring refraction by the cornea/lens, cutting off peripheral paraxial rays and increasing depth of focus. Uses & Interpretation: Differentiates refractive errors from organic media opacities or retinal/macular diseases. Vision improves with Pinhole: Indicates a refractive error (correctable up to ±3 Diopters; very high refractive errors like -10 D or aphakia +10 D will not fully correct with a pinhole alone). Vision worsens with Pinhole: Indicates macular pathology (e.g., macular edema, CSR, ARMD) or central media opacity (e.g., central corneal opacity, posterior subcapsular cataract).

q: Thin at centre, thick at periphery; forms a minified, erect, virtual image; image moves WITH lens movement. Example trial lens shown: -2.25 D
u: Correction of myopia; Hruby lens (-58.6 D) and fundus contact lens uses (see added note).
note: Spherical Concave Lens (Minus Lens) — Identification: 1. Image Size: Forms a minified (smaller), erect, virtual image. 2. Movement Test: When the lens is moved, the image moves WITH the movement of the lens. 3. Palpation: Thin at the center, thick at the periphery. Uses in Ophthalmology: 1. Therapeutic: Correction of Myopia. 2. Diagnostic: Hruby Lens (-58.6 D): Planoconcave lens attached to the slit lamp for fundus biomicroscopy. Fundus Contact Lens (e.g., Goldmann 3-mirror lens uses a central -64 D lens to neutralize corneal refractive power).

q: Thick at centre, thin at periphery; magnified image when held close (inverted beyond focal length); image moves AGAINST lens movement. Example trial lens shown: +14.00 D
u: Correction of hypermetropia, presbyopia and aphakia; +20 D indirect ophthalmoscope, +90 D / +78 D slit-lamp lenses, and other instruments (see added note).
note: Spherical Convex Lens (Plus Lens) — Identification: 1. Image Size: Forms a magnified (enlarged) image when held close to the object (becomes inverted if held beyond its focal length). 2. Movement Test: When the lens is moved, the image moves AGAINST the movement of the lens. 3. Palpation: Thick at the center, thin at the periphery. Uses in Ophthalmology: 1. Therapeutic/Refractive: Correction of Hypermetropia, Presbyopia, and Aphakia (high plus lens, approx. +10 D). 2. Diagnostic & Optical Instruments: Indirect Ophthalmoscope: Uses a +20 D condensing lens. Slit-Lamp Fundus Biomicroscopy: Uses +90 D or +78 D non-contact condensing lenses. Used in Direct Ophthalmoscope, Retinoscope, Synoptophore, Slit Lamp, Operating Microscope, Keratometer, and Surgical Loupes.

q: Image not verified — text only. Usually no handle; two etched markings on rim indicating axis; no power along axis, maximum power perpendicular (90 degrees) to axis; rotation gives scissoring/swirling distortion.
u: Correction of astigmatism (myopic or hypermetropic).
note: Cylindrical Lens — Identification: 1. Usually has no handle and features two etched markings on the rim indicating the Axis. 2. Power Orientation: There is no power along the axis (it is plane along the axis); maximum refractive power is perpendicular (90 degrees) to the axis. 3. Movement & Rotation Test: Moving the lens along the axis produces no image movement; moving it perpendicular to the axis produces WITH (minus cylinder) or AGAINST (plus cylinder) movement. Rotating the lens causes a characteristic "scissoring" or "optical swirling" distortion of the image. Use: Correction of Astigmatism (Myopic or Hypermetropic astigmatism).

n: Bimanual I/A cannulas + Coaxial I/A handpiece
q: Image not verified — text only. Bimanual: two separate handpieces through two side-ports. Coaxial: single probe combining irrigation sleeve and central aspiration tip.
u: Bimanual and coaxial irrigation/aspiration for cortical wash in phacoemulsification (see added note for the distinction).
note: Irrigation/Aspiration (I/A) Cannulas — 1. Bimanual Irrigation & Aspiration (I/A) Cannulas: Design: Two separate handpieces introduced through two side-ports in Phacoemulsification: Irrigation Handpiece: Has two side openings for fluid inflow. Aspiration Handpiece: Has a single 0.3 mm opening at the tip to aspirate residual cortical matter (especially sub-incisional cortex). 2. Coaxial I/A Handpiece: Design: Combines both irrigation (via an outer silicone sleeve with two side ports) and aspiration (via a central metal tip) into a single probe introduced through the main corneal incision. This card is distinct from the Simcoe two-way cannula card. Ball-point cautery is on card 35 (Thermocautery), not on this card.

q: Image not verified — text only. Whatman No. 41 filter paper, 5 mm wide x 35 mm long, fold/notch at 5 mm, graduated scale 5 to 35 mm.
u: Schirmer tear test: folded 5 mm end in lower fornix for 5 minutes; normal > 15 mm, dry eye < 10 mm, severe < 5 mm (see added note).
note: Schirmer's Tear Test Strip — Material & Dimensions: Whatman No. 41 filter paper, measuring 5 mm wide x 35 mm long, with a fold/notch at 5 mm and a graduated millimeter scale (5 to 35 mm). Procedure: The folded 5 mm end is hooked into the lower conjunctival fornix at the junction of the middle and lateral one-third of the lower eyelid (avoiding corneal contact) for 5 minutes. Types: Without Topical Anesthesia (Schirmer I): Measures total tear secretion (both basal and reflex secretion). With Topical Anesthesia: Measures basal tear secretion only. Interpretation (Wetting at 5 minutes): Normal: > 15 mm (10-15 mm is borderline). Dry Eye: < 10 mm (< 5 mm indicates severe dry eye).

q: Image not verified — text only. Water-soluble orange-red dye strip; fluoresces bright green under cobalt blue filter.
u: Staining corneal epithelial defects/ulcers/abrasions; Goldmann applanation tonometry; Seidel's test; tear film break-up time; fundus fluorescein angiography (see added note).
note: Fluorescein Sodium Strip (1 mg / 2%) — Principle: Water-soluble orange-red dye that fluoresces bright green when illuminated with a Cobalt Blue filter on the slit lamp. Uses: 1. Staining Corneal Epithelial Defects / Corneal Ulcers / Abrasions: Intact corneal epithelium is lipid-rich (hydrophobic) and repels fluorescein. Where the epithelium is breached, the water-soluble dye penetrates and stains the hydrophilic corneal stroma bright green. 2. Goldmann Applanation Tonometry (GAT): Stains the tear film to form two bright green semicircular mires viewed through the doubling prism of the applanation tonometer to measure IOP accurately. 3. Seidel's Test: Detects aqueous humor leak from the anterior chamber (e.g., perforating corneal injury or post-operative wound leak after cataract/trabeculectomy surgery). Leaking aqueous dilutes the dark orange concentrated dye into a bright green flowing stream under cobalt blue light. 4. Tear Film Break-Up Time (TBUT): Evaluates Dry Eye Disease (specifically mucin/lipid layer instability). After instilling fluorescein, the patient blinks once and keeps the eye open; the time taken for the first dry black spot to appear in the green tear film is measured (Normal: > 10 seconds; < 10 seconds is abnormal). 5. Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Uses intravenous injection of 5 mL of 10% (or 3 mL of 20%) sterile Fluorescein Sodium into the antecubital vein followed by serial fundus photography. Evaluates retinal and choroidal vasculature (arm-to-retina circulation time, capillary non-perfusion areas, microaneurysms, neovascularization, vascular occlusions, and macular leakage in Diabetic Retinopathy, CRVO/BRVO, ARMD, etc.

q: Image not verified — text only. Small lightweight forceps, 1:2 teeth, straight/curved/angular — see yellow note for full iridectomy method
u: See yellow note
note: General Iris Forceps note (general, not Bishop-Harmon; full transcription copied from card 27): Iris Forceps — Identification: It is a small lightweight forceps with 1:2 teeth on the inner side of its tips. If the limb is closed, teeth cannot be seen or felt. The shape of the forceps may be straight, curved or angular. Method of Iridectomy: a) Hold the instrument in such a way that its tips face towards 12 o'clock position and angle towards 6 o'clock position. b) Now enter into the AC with closed tip and touch the peripheral iris. c) Open the forceps a little to catch a pinch of iris tissue and take out a triangular fold of iris outside the section. d) Cut a small triangular piece of iris radially with Wecker's scissors. Always check the severed iris tissue by rubbing it over face mask. This is to see if the pigmented layer has been cut or not, i.e., if there is release of pigment - it means iridectomy has been done in full thickness. Types of Iridectomy: 1. Peripheral button-hole iridectomy: (at 11 and/or 1 o'clock position) one full-thickness iridectomy is equally effective as two iridectomies. The indications are: a) In intracapsular cataract extraction (not mandatory in extracapsular cataract extraction). b) Angle closure glaucoma. c) As a part of trabeculectomy operation. d) In penetrating keratoplasty operation. Peripheral iridectomy is done to prevent pupillary block glaucoma and consequent iris prolapse in case of ICCE. As the aqueous can flow into the anterior chamber via this bypass channel, equilibrium between the anterior chamber and posterior chamber is maintained after ICCE. 2. Optical iridectomy: In case of central corneal opacity where facilities for keratoplasty are not available and rarely in polar cataracts. It is done in the lower part of the iris, as in the upper part, the new opening will be covered by upper lid. The best site for optical iridectomy is judged by stenopaic slit test, and it must be at the clearest zone. Customarily, it is said that the site of election will be down and in for the literates, and down and out for illiterates. 3. Glaucoma iridectomy or Iridectomy dialysis: Done in congestive glaucoma to facilitate drainage of aqueous. Here, iris is torn from its root instead of cutting it with the scissors. 4. Broad or Complete iridectomy: To facilitate the extraction of lens (combined extraction of cataract) when pupil is small and rigid, or if there is extensive synechiae, and if there is vitreous loss after cataract extraction. Indications: a) Iridectomy for prolapsed iris. b) Iridectomy to remove foreign body on the iris. c) Iridectomy to remove tumour or cyst. 5. Preliminary iridectomy: It is a test iridectomy, in uveitis causing complicated cataract, in the first sitting to see the reaction in that eye. 6. Involuntary iridectomy: It is the iridectomy caused by a cataract knife during 'ab-interno' section, when the AC becomes shallow or aqueous gets drained out early before completing the section. Here, there is no need for forceps or Wecker's scissors; YAG laser peripheral iridectomy is better in acute attack of ACG as it is a non-invasive (so no chance of infection) and cheap OPD procedure.
